children.text: The video as a whole can be seen as a mild but clear example of ragebait. Joey does not generate controversy himself. He chooses an already divisive video and profits off of it. This is a much safer way to use ragebait to farm engagement. Many ragebait creators receive a lot of hate, and this does not lead to a loyal fanbase. By instead commenting on ragebait, Joey is able to build his own fanbase. By the time Joey actually enters the video after 35 seconds, he is mostly restating the ideas that the audience already formed. Rather than offering fresh insight, he uses sarcasm to provide the general consensus.

The beginning of the video lays the groundwork for the rest of the video. The video that Joey is commenting on plays almost in its entirety, so that the audience has context. By starting with this and not his own commentary, Joey allows the viewer to build their own opinion first. Since their opinion most likely aligns with what he is about to say, it builds his credibility. The video depicts a man in the gym doing curls. He is then approached and asked how many sets he has left. This method of giving the viewer context only works due to one of TikTok’s affordances, the stitch feature. He is able to directly attach his commentary to the video.

When Joey appears in the video, he is in his car. He is not in the gym or a branded set. This gives the video a feeling of immediately needing to be recorded. He did not wait to get home, instead he recorded the video right where he was. This better frames his commentary as authentic rather than being actually produced. The viewer is better able to see Joey as a relatable person rather than a big-time creator. After gaining this trust, viewers give more weight to the rest of the video since audiences tend to trust real people rather than manufactured content creators.

Throughout his commentary, Joey addresses the original creator’s video rather than the audience. His sarcastic use of bro and his eventual suggestion of building a home gym are framed as him talking directly to the stitched creator rather than his audience. Addressing the creator instead of the audience is an intentional choice by Joey. He positions the audience as passively witnessing someone being corrected rather than being the targets of Joey’s persuasion. This makes the video seem less like an attempt to change the mind of the viewers and instead as engaging in an argument which they agree with. This helps reinforce Joey’s loyalty.

Right after his entrance, Joey repeatedly says the word “bro.” He is mimicking the same way that the original creator speaks. By starting with this intonation and repeated mocking, Joey makes it clear that he has a negative view point on the video he is stitching. This also primes the audience for the somewhat condescending tone that he speaks with. He uses a negative view because he is responding to the original ragebait video. He knows that the audience is probably already upset at the creator so he plays into it. By opening with distinct ridicule rather than a measured argument, he plays into the same ragebait genre.

In this part of the video Joey Swoll continues to talk sarcastically while explaining the concept of the “gym.” He explains that the gym is a shared space; therefore, the creator’s behavior is unwarranted and rude. He appeals to the common sense of the viewer to recognize proper gym etiquette. By framing his commentary as a necessary correction rather than just a general critique, Joey formalizes gym etiquette and identifies this breach. This sarcastic delivery keeps his video in line with how he starts the section with his mocking tone. This combination allows him to keep logic at the forefront while also underlining it with a mocking sarcastic tone.

After explaining how to properly act in the public setting, Joey then says that if the creator did want to act that way then he should build a private gym. The idea of building a home gym, which is incredibly unrealistic and expensive for most people, causes the creator’s suggestion to seem even more idiotic. By framing all of the things that the creator is negatively reacting to as very reasonable things, he paints him in an even more absurd light. Additionally, Joey appeals directly to his gym-going audience. Many people in his audience have most likely also been approached with a similar question and would never think of reacting the way the original creator did.

Joey ends the video by saying until then mind your business and do better. He ends with one final dig at the creator and urges him to improve going forward. After critiquing this creator the entire video and painting him in a bad light, Joey does one final jab at them that is purely emotion based. He abandons the logical reasoning he had been using in the video thus far. This pathos driven attack mimics the creator’s own rhetoric. His short closing line is extremely direct and condenses the point of his video down into a single moment. This makes it more effective for engagement without necessarily adding any new material.
